back: Small n can permit exhaustive search, but estimate actual output: 10! = 3,628,800 and 12! = 479,001,600 permutations. Copying/storing each permutation adds O(n) work and space per result. n <= 12 is not a runtime guarantee.
reason: Original factorial cutoff presents a potentially enormous workload as reliably feasible.

back: Small n can permit subset enumeration or bitmask DP, but 2^20 is about 1 million and 2^25 about 33.6 million states. Multiply by transition/copy cost and check memory. O(n·2^n) is materially larger than O(2^n).
reason: Original cutoff omits transition and materialized-output costs.

back: Estimate loops: 100^3 is 1 million, while 100^4 is 100 million iterations. Some cubic algorithms fit; quartic work may not. A 2-D DP is often O(mn), not inherently cubic or quartic.
reason: Original answer incorrectly associates dimensionality of DP with cubic/quartic complexity.

back: 500^3 is 125 million iterations, so cubic work needs a careful time-limit and transition-cost check. Treat it as a rough candidate, not a safe rule. Also estimate table memory.
reason: Original cubic cutoff is too categorical.

back: Quadratic work is about 25 million iterations at n=5,000. That may fit simple loops, but a full 5,000×5,000 int table alone uses about 100 MB. Check both time and memory.
reason: Original answer omits large quadratic storage cost.

back: O(n log n) is often a reasonable target around n=100,000; O(n^2) is about 10 billion iterations. Sorting, heaps, and balanced trees are candidates when their invariants match the task. Complexity cutoffs remain estimates.
reason: Qualifies heuristic cutoff without changing its useful comparison.

back: At millions of items, aim for a small number of linear passes when possible. A ten-million-element int array alone has about 40 MB of payload; O(n) maps can be much larger. Hashing, windows, and prefix sums each need the right contract.
reason: Original answer treats every linear approach as equally feasible.

back: If 10^9 or 10^18 is a numeric answer range, consider math or binary search on a proven monotone predicate. If n is actual explicit input length, reading it already costs Ω(n). Search cost also includes the cost of each predicate evaluation.
reason: Distinguishes input length from numeric answer range; original conflates them.

back: Consider a variable window only if validity and boundary movement have a monotone relationship. Longest-valid windows often expand, shrink while invalid, then measure. Shortest-valid windows often measure and shrink while valid. Negative-sum constraints may need prefix sums instead.
reason: Original blanket substring trigger and loop direction are not generally correct.

back: Compare character frequencies for O(n) expected time, or O(n) with a fixed declared alphabet. int[26] requires lowercase ASCII a-z. Sorting is also correct (O(n log n)); it is a tradeoff, not forbidden.
reason: Original incorrectly forbids a correct sorting approach and omits alphabet contract.

back: Use a monotonic stack of indices, with the comparator and output tailored to the question. Next strictly greater pops smaller values; daily temperatures writes i-poppedIndex; stock span pops previous values <= current and measures distance to the previous greater value.
reason: Stock span and next-greater require different output/comparison details.

back: Binary search a proven monotone answer predicate. Shipping and nonnegative contiguous splitting use greedy capacity checks. Eating-speed tasks sum ceiling(pile/speed). Establish feasible bounds and use wide arithmetic; these predicates are not interchangeable.
reason: Distinguishes capacity packing from eating-speed feasibility.

back: Use BFS or DFS flood fill for each unvisited land component. Mark when scheduling/entering a cell. In-place marking saves a separate visited array only when mutation is allowed; an explicit stack avoids deep recursion.
reason: Original recommends mutation without a permission/contract qualifier.

back: Use Dijkstra for nonnegative edge weights. Equal-cost edges can use BFS. Negative edges may require Bellman-Ford with reachable negative-cycle handling, or topological relaxation in a DAG. A relevant reachable negative cycle means no finite shortest path.
reason: Dijkstra needs nonnegative weights; negative cycles invalidate a finite answer.

back: Use a trie for shared-prefix queries. A node can hold 26 children plus an end-of-word flag only with a lowercase ASCII a-z contract; use a suitable mapping for a broader alphabet. A HashSet is often simpler for exact membership alone.
reason: Original assumes a fixed alphabet without stating it.

back: Define a precise DP state first, then enumerate legal final decisions and base cases. Minimum stair cost can use min(dp[i-1]+cost[i-1], dp[i-2]+cost[i-2]); a different profit/cost problem may need entirely different state.
reason: Original trigger is too broad to identify a universal recurrence.

back: For unlimited positive denominations, dp[amount] = min(dp[amount-coin]+1) over legal coins, with dp[0]=0. In a coin-outer compressed DP, forward capacities allow reuse. Counting combinations versus sequences requires different loop ordering.
reason: Original forward-loop rule omits state and counting semantics.

back: General binary tree: recurse, return a target node when found, and return the current node when both child calls find a target. This concise version assumes both target references exist. BST with known-present unique keys: walk until the values split around the current node.
reason: Original LCA answer omits the target-presence assumption.

back: Floyd cycle detection using values as next indices works for n+1 entries, values in 1..n, and exactly one distinct duplicate. It finds the cycle entry without mutation. Arbitrary arrays do not meet this contract.
reason: Original array-cycle trigger omits essential constraints.

back: Boyer-Moore voting finds a candidate by canceling unequal pairs. If a strict majority is not guaranteed, make a second pass to verify its count exceeds n/2. Empty/no-majority input needs an explicit absence result.
reason: Original voting answer omits required candidate verification.

back: Choose a proven constant-space approach under the actual contract: two-pointer compaction, in-place swapping, or index marking when values map to valid indices and mutation is allowed. Negation marking needs positive-domain/zero/overflow care. O(1) alone does not identify a pattern.
reason: Original suggests unsafe marking without domain constraints.
Original counting loop is ambiguous about levels versus edge distance and lacks usable endpoint/wall contract; guide supplies full method.

back: BFS gives shortest paths in equal-cost/unweighted graphs. Ordinary DFS finds a path, but its first path need not be shortest. Nonnegative unequal weights -> Dijkstra; negative edges require a different algorithm and cycle handling.
reason: Original weighted->Dijkstra rule lacks nonnegative constraint.

back: In the standard longest-valid-window template, right advances once per outer loop; shrink left with while until validity is restored, then measure. Shortest-valid windows often measure and shrink while valid. Some specialized windows legitimately use a single if; follow the invariant, not a blanket rule.
reason: Original never-if advice and universal shrink direction are false.

back: Recursion depth can be O(n) on a skewed tree/list or thin grid component. Safe depth depends on runtime stack and frame size; there is no universal node cutoff. Use an explicit stack or iterative DP when depth may be large.
reason: Original stack-overflow cutoff is stated as certainty.

back: Many collection mutations invalidate foreach enumeration, but exact behavior depends on collection, operation, and runtime. A reliable general pattern is to iterate a snapshot of keys (new List<TKey>(d.Keys)) and apply changes to the original, or collect changes and apply afterward.
reason: Original blanket exception claim is false for some modern Dictionary operations.

back: Think aloud at useful decision points: state assumptions, explain an invariant, describe why a plan failed, and narrate test results. Short quiet thinking is normal; there is no universal 20-second rule or guarantee an interviewer will hint.
reason: Original makes unsupported universal claims about interviewer behavior.

back: Before coding, clarify the contract, give a correct baseline, explain the key invariant, and state expected time/space. Check for questions when useful, then implement and test purposeful edge cases. A ritual permission request is not required in every interview.
reason: Original presents a particular communication script as a universal senior signal.
